options.text: The header name is invalid, because custom headers must not start with `X-`
options.why: The `X-` prefix is discouraged by RFC 6648 but still perfectly legal in Node.

options.text: `setHeader` runs after `res.end()` has already sent the headers
options.why: Headers go out with the first body bytes or at `end()`; after that they can't change.

options.text: The client closed the connection before the server could reply
options.why: A disconnect produces `ECONNRESET` or a `close` event, not this error.

options.text: Node needs `res.writeHead()` to be called before `setHeader()` can be used
options.why: `setHeader` works without `writeHead`; calling it after `writeHead` is what fails.

explanation: Node sends the status line and headers once: on `res.writeHead()`, on the first `res.write()`, or at `res.end()`. Any later `setHeader`, `writeHead` or Express `res.status().send()` throws `ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT`. In Express the same error usually means a handler sent two responses, for example `res.send()` and then `next()`, or a missing `return`.

stem: In Node.js, `await fetch(url)` rejects when the server answers with `404 Not Found` or `500 Internal Server Error`.

options.text: True
options.why: fetch only rejects for network-level failures such as DNS errors, refused connections or aborts.

options.text: False
options.why: Any HTTP response resolves; check `response.ok` or `response.status` yourself.

explanation: The WHATWG fetch that Node ships (built on undici) resolves for every HTTP response, including 4xx and 5xx. `response.ok` is true only for statuses 200 to 299. Code that does `const data = await (await fetch(url)).json()` without checking `ok` will happily try to parse an error page.

stem: An Express 5 app uses `app.use(express.json())` with no options. Clients posting large JSON documents get an error. What is the default body size `limit` of `express.json()`? Type the value as Express writes it (for example `1mb`).
explanation: The JSON, urlencoded and text parsers default to `limit: '100kb'`. Bigger bodies fail with an error whose `status` is 413 and `type` is `entity.too.large`. Raise the limit per route, for example `express.json({ limit: '5mb' })` on the import endpoint only, instead of globally, so other routes keep a small attack surface.

stem: Match each `http.Server` setting with what it limits. Defaults shown are for Node.js 22 and 24.

options.text: How long an idle keep-alive connection is held open after a response (5 s)
How long the client may take to send the complete request headers (60 s)
How long the client may take to send the entire request, headers and body (300 s)
The socket inactivity timeout, disabled by default (0)

explanation: These are separate knobs. `keepAliveTimeout` (5000 ms) closes idle persistent connections. `headersTimeout` (60000 ms) and `requestTimeout` (300000 ms) protect against slow clients such as Slowloris and answer `408 Request Timeout`. `server.timeout` is the per-socket inactivity timeout and is `0` (off) by default. None of them limits how long your handler may take to respond.

options.text: `writeHead` must be called after `write`, so the status line is never sent
options.why: The order shown is correct; `writeHead` before `write` is the normal pattern.

options.text: `res.write` only accepts Buffers, so the string is silently dropped
options.why: `write` accepts strings and Buffers; the text does reach the client.

options.text: The response is never finished, because nothing calls `res.end()`
options.why: Without `end()` the chunked response stays open, so the client keeps waiting for more.

options.text: Plain-text responses need a `Content-Length` header or Node refuses to send them
options.why: Without a length Node uses chunked transfer encoding automatically.

explanation: `res.write()` sends a chunk; only `res.end()` marks the response complete. Because no `Content-Length` is known, Node uses `Transfer-Encoding: chunked`, and the client waits for the final zero-length chunk that `end()` would send. Every code path, including errors, must end the response.

stem: Which statements about the global `fetch` in Node.js 22 and 24 are true? (Choose three.)

options.text: It is available without importing anything
options.why: fetch has been global and stable since Node 21 (experimental from 18).

options.text: It is implemented by the undici HTTP client
options.why: Node bundles undici and exposes its fetch, Request, Response and Headers globally.

options.text: It follows redirects by default
options.why: The default `redirect: 'follow'` follows up to 20 redirects; use `'manual'` to inspect them.

options.text: It rejects the promise for any status code of 400 or above
options.why: It resolves for every HTTP response; only network errors and aborts reject.

options.text: It stores cookies from responses and sends them on later requests
options.why: Node's fetch has no cookie jar; you must forward `Set-Cookie` values yourself.

options.text: It uses the same `http.globalAgent` sockets as `http.request`
options.why: undici manages its own connection pool, separate from the `node:http` agents.

explanation: Node's fetch follows the WHATWG spec where it can: global, promise-based, redirect-following, and resolving for HTTP errors. Server-side differences matter: there is no cookie jar and no CORS enforcement, and connections come from undici's own pool, which you tune with an undici `Agent` passed as `dispatcher`, not with `http.Agent`.

options.text: Express 5 removed `express.json()`; you must install `body-parser` separately
options.why: `express.json()` is still built in; it wraps body-parser for you.

options.text: Middleware runs in order, and the parser is registered after the route
options.why: The route answers before `express.json()` ever runs, so the body is never parsed.

options.text: `req.body` is only filled for `PUT` and `PATCH`, not for `POST` requests
options.why: Body parsers work for any method that has a body, including POST.

options.text: The parser needs `extended: true` to handle nested JSON objects
options.why: `extended` is an option of `express.urlencoded()`, not of the JSON parser.

explanation: Express builds one stack in the order of `app.use` and `app.get/post` calls and walks it per request. A route that sends a response ends the walk, so later middleware never runs for it. Register parsers, logging, auth and CORS before the routes that need them, and error handlers last.

stem: A dashboard only needs the server to push price updates to the browser; the browser never sends messages back. The team wants automatic reconnection and to keep plain HTTP infrastructure. Which transport fits best?

options.text: Server-Sent Events over a long-lived HTTP response
options.why: One-way server push over HTTP, and the browser's EventSource reconnects automatically.

options.text: WebSockets, because only they can push data without a request
options.why: WebSockets work, but they add a protocol upgrade and two-way framing that this case doesn't need.

options.text: Short polling every second with `setInterval` and `fetch`
options.why: Polling adds latency and load and isn't real push.

options.text: HTTP/2 server push of each update as a separate resource
options.why: HTTP/2 push was for preloading assets; browsers have removed support for it.

explanation: SSE (`Content-Type: text/event-stream`) is a single streaming HTTP response the server keeps writing to. The browser's `EventSource` handles reconnection and `Last-Event-ID` resumption, and it passes through ordinary HTTP proxies and load balancers. Pick WebSockets when you need low-latency messages in both directions.

stem: In Express 5, which of these errors reach the app's 4-argument error handler without any extra code? (Choose two.)

options.text: An error thrown inside an `async` route handler
options.why: Express 5 catches the returned promise's rejection and calls `next(err)` for you.

options.text: A rejected promise returned from a non-async handler
options.why: Any returned promise that rejects is forwarded to the error handler.

options.text: An error thrown inside a `setTimeout` callback started by a handler
options.why: The throw happens later on a fresh call stack; it becomes an `uncaughtException`.

options.text: An `error` event emitted by a stream the handler piped into `res`
options.why: Stream errors need their own listener or `stream.pipeline` with a callback.

options.text: An error thrown in a callback passed to `fs.readFile`
options.why: Callback errors run outside Express's promise; call `next(err)` yourself.

explanation: Express 5 wraps handlers so that a synchronous throw, a thrown error in an `async` function, or a returned rejected promise all end up in `next(err)`. Anything that fails on a different call stack, such as timers, callbacks or event emitters, is invisible to Express. Convert it to a promise (`await setTimeout()` from `timers/promises`, `fs.promises`, `stream/promises`) or pass the error to `next` yourself.

options.text: Error handlers must be registered with `app.error()` instead of `app.use()`
options.why: There is no `app.error`; error handlers are added with `app.use` like other middleware.

options.text: `res.json()` cannot be used in error handlers; only `res.send()` works there
options.why: Any response method works in an error handler.

options.text: Express recognises error handlers by having exactly four parameters
options.why: With three it is treated as normal middleware, which Express skips while an error is pending.

options.text: The handler must call `next()` at the end, or Express ignores its response
options.why: Calling `next()` after responding would pass the request on, not make this one count.

explanation: Express checks the function's `length`. A function declared `(err, req, res, next)` is an error handler; `(err, req, res)` looks like `(req, res, next)` with odd names and is skipped when `next(err)` is called. Keep the fourth parameter even if you never use it, and register error handlers after all routes.

stem: An Express app runs behind an Nginx reverse proxy that sets `X-Forwarded-For`. `trust proxy` is not configured. A rate limiter keys on `req.ip`. What happens?

options.text: Each user is limited individually, because Express reads `X-Forwarded-For` by default
options.why: Express ignores forwarding headers unless `trust proxy` is set.

options.text: Every user shares one bucket, because `req.ip` is the proxy's address
options.why: All requests arrive from Nginx, so one busy user throttles everyone.

options.text: Requests are rejected, because Express refuses to serve untrusted forwarding headers
options.why: Express doesn't reject them; it just doesn't use them for `req.ip`.

options.text: `req.ip` is undefined, so the limiter skips the check entirely
options.why: `req.ip` is always set to the socket's remote address when no proxy is trusted.

explanation: With the default `trust proxy` of `false`, `req.ip` is the TCP peer, which is the proxy. Set `app.set('trust proxy', 1)` (one hop) or the proxy's address range, so that Express takes the client address from `X-Forwarded-For` and the scheme from `X-Forwarded-Proto`. Don't set it to `true` when clients can reach the app directly, because then anyone can forge the header.

stem: An Express app sets `app.set('trust proxy', 1)`. A request arrives from the load balancer with `X-Forwarded-For: 1.2.3.4, 5.6.7.8`. What is `req.ip`? Type the address.
explanation: Each proxy appends the address it received the request from, so the right-most entry was added by the hop nearest your server. Trusting 1 hop means Express trusts the load balancer and takes the entry it appended: `5.6.7.8`. The left-most value, `1.2.3.4`, was supplied by an earlier party and could be forged. Set the hop count to match your real topology.

stem: A service calls an upstream with `http.get` through `new http.Agent({ keepAlive: true, maxSockets: 10 })`. For some status codes the callback returns early without reading the response body. Which two things follow? (Choose two.)

options.text: The socket stays busy and isn't returned to the pool
options.why: An unread body keeps the socket occupied, so the agent can't reuse it.

options.text: Once 10 sockets are stuck, new requests queue and hang
options.why: Requests beyond `maxSockets` wait for a free socket that never comes.

options.text: Node discards the body automatically after the callback returns
options.why: Node never drains bodies for you; call `res.resume()` to discard one.

options.text: Node closes the socket and opens a new one, so only latency suffers
options.why: The socket isn't closed; it sits there with unread data.

options.text: Node throws `ERR_STREAM_PREMATURE_CLOSE` on the next request
options.why: No error is thrown; the symptom is silent queuing.

explanation: An `IncomingMessage` is a readable stream. Until it is fully read, the socket can't carry another request, so the agent doesn't put it back in its free pool. Always consume the body (`res.resume()` to discard it, or read it). The same applies to fetch: read or cancel `response.body` when you don't need it.

options.text: Node sends TCP data in UTF-16, so the bytes need decoding first
options.why: Strings are sent as UTF-8 by default, and that would fail every time, not sometimes.

options.text: TCP has no message boundaries; one `data` event held both messages
options.why: Writes aren't message boundaries; here both arrived as `{"a":1}{"b":2}`.

options.text: The second `write` was dropped because the first hadn't been acknowledged
options.why: TCP is reliable and ordered; no bytes are dropped.

options.text: `data` events fire before the socket is ready, so the JSON is truncated
options.why: Data events only fire once bytes have actually arrived.

explanation: TCP guarantees order and delivery, not boundaries. The OS can merge small writes (Nagle's algorithm) or split large ones, so your protocol must add framing: newline-delimited JSON with a line buffer, or a length prefix (for example a 4-byte size before each message), and a parser that buffers partial frames. HTTP, WebSockets and gRPC all do this for you.

stem: Put the middleware of an Express 5 JSON API in the order it should be registered.

options.text: `app.use(express.json())`
`app.use(requireAuth)`
`app.post('/orders', createOrder)`
`app.use((req, res) => res.status(404).json({ error: 'Not found' }))`
`app.use((err, req, res, next) => res.status(err.status ?? 500).json({ error: err.message }))`

explanation: Express runs middleware in registration order. Parse bodies first so later code can read `req.body`, then authenticate, then the routes. A catch-all 404 handler goes after every route, because it only runs when nothing matched. The 4-argument error handler goes last, so errors from anything above reach it.
reference: Express docs: Using middleware; Error handling

options.text: Node serializes the object with `JSON.stringify` and sends `{"ok":true}`
options.why: Only Express's `res.json` serializes; core `res.end` doesn't.

options.text: The client receives the string `[object Object]`
options.why: Node doesn't call `toString` on the chunk; it validates the type first.

options.text: `res.end` throws `ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE`; it only takes strings or Buffers
options.why: Core streams only accept a string, Buffer or Uint8Array as a chunk.

options.text: The response ends with an empty body, because objects are ignored
options.why: The call throws rather than silently dropping the value.

explanation: `node:http` is low-level. You must serialize yourself: `res.end(JSON.stringify(data))`. Express adds `res.json()`, which serializes, sets `Content-Type` and handles `ETag`. Mixing the two mental models is a common source of crashes when code moves from Express to a raw handler or vice versa.

stem: In Node.js 20 and later, outbound requests made with `http.request` through the default `http.globalAgent` reuse keep-alive connections by default.

options.text: True
options.why: Since Node 19 the global agents are created with `keepAlive: true`.

options.text: False
options.why: This was true before Node 19, when every request opened and closed its own connection.

explanation: Node 19 changed `http.globalAgent` and `https.globalAgent` to keep connections alive, with `maxFreeSockets` of 256 and no `maxSockets` limit. This speeds up service-to-service calls, but it also exposes the keep-alive race: the server may close an idle socket just as the client reuses it, which shows up as occasional `ECONNRESET`.
reference: Node.js docs: http.globalAgent; Node 19 release notes

stem: After upgrading from Express 4 to Express 5, the app crashes on startup with `Missing parameter name at index 1: *`. Which route causes it, and what is the fix?

options.text: `app.get('/users/:id')`; parameters must now be written as `{id}`
options.why: Named `:id` parameters work unchanged in Express 5.

options.text: `app.get('*')`; wildcards must be named, as in `app.get('/*splat')`
options.why: path-to-regexp 8 needs a name for every wildcard; `req.params.splat` then holds the segments.

options.text: `app.use(express.static('public'))`; static paths need a trailing `*`
options.why: Static middleware doesn't use route patterns and needs no wildcard.

options.text: `app.get('/files/:name.pdf')`; dots are no longer allowed in paths
options.why: Literal characters such as dots are still allowed next to parameters.

explanation: Express 5 uses path-to-regexp 8, which dropped unnamed wildcards and regex-like syntax. `*` becomes `/*splat` (one or more segments, returned as an array) or `/{*splat}` to also match the root. Optional segments use braces, as in `/:file{.:ext}`. Run the official codemods or search for `'*'` and `?` in route strings when upgrading.

options.text: `express.json()` never reports oversized bodies; it truncates them silently
options.why: It rejects them with an error object rather than truncating.

options.text: The handler ignores `err.status`, which body-parser sets to 413
options.why: The error has `status: 413` and `type: 'entity.too.large'`; the handler overwrites it with 500.

options.text: A 413 can only be sent by the reverse proxy, not by Node
options.why: Node can send any status; body-parser raises a 413 error for Express to send.

options.text: The handler must call `next(err)` so Express adds the right status
options.why: Calling `next(err)` would fall through to the default handler, not fix this one.

explanation: Errors from Express middleware usually carry an HTTP status: body-parser uses 413 for oversized bodies and 400 (`entity.parse.failed`) for malformed JSON. A generic handler should respect it: `res.status(err.status ?? err.statusCode ?? 500)`. Otherwise client mistakes look like server crashes in your monitoring.

stem: A Node.js API runs behind an AWS Application Load Balancer with the default 60-second idle timeout. Under moderate traffic, about 0.1% of requests fail with `502 Bad Gateway`, and the Node logs show no errors for them. The server uses default settings. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The handler takes more than 60 seconds, so the ALB gives up on it
options.why: Slow handlers produce 504 Gateway Timeout, and they would show up in your latency metrics.

options.text: Node closes idle keep-alive sockets after 5 s, while the ALB may reuse them for 60 s
options.why: The ALB sends a request just as Node closes the socket, and gets a reset, which it turns into a 502.

options.text: The ALB opens too many connections and Node's `maxConnections` limit rejects them
options.why: `maxConnections` is unlimited by default, and rejections would be logged.

options.text: Node's `requestTimeout` of 300 s is longer than the ALB timeout, so the ALB rejects it
options.why: `requestTimeout` only limits how long the client takes to send the request.

explanation: The ALB keeps connections to targets open for up to its idle timeout (60 s) and reuses them. Node's `keepAliveTimeout` defaults to 5 s, so Node closes idle sockets first. When a request races with that close, the ALB sees a TCP reset and returns 502 without the request reaching your code. Set `server.keepAliveTimeout` longer than the load balancer's idle timeout (for example 65 s), and keep `headersTimeout` above it as well.
reference: AWS docs: ALB connection idle timeout; Node.js docs: server.keepAliveTimeout

stem: Kubernetes sends `SIGTERM` to a Node.js API pod during a rolling deploy and kills it 30 seconds later. Which steps belong in a correct graceful shutdown? (Choose three.)

options.text: Call `server.close()` to stop accepting new connections
options.why: New connections are refused, while existing ones are allowed to finish.

options.text: Let in-flight requests finish, then close database pools and exit
options.why: Closing pools too early fails the requests that are still running.

options.text: After a deadline under 30 s, call `server.closeAllConnections()` and exit anyway
options.why: A hard deadline makes sure the pod exits before Kubernetes sends SIGKILL.

options.text: Call `process.exit(0)` immediately so the new pod starts sooner
options.why: Exiting at once drops every in-flight request, which is what graceful shutdown avoids.

options.text: Ignore SIGTERM and wait for SIGKILL, so no request is ever cut short
options.why: SIGKILL can't be handled, so in-flight work is lost without any cleanup.

options.text: Restart the server on a new port so that load balancer health checks keep passing
options.why: That keeps sending traffic to a pod that is being removed.

explanation: A solid sequence: fail readiness checks so no new traffic is routed, call `server.close()` (in Node 19+ this also closes idle keep-alive sockets), wait for in-flight requests, close pools and queues, then exit. Always add a hard deadline that force-closes remaining connections, because a slow client or a hung request would otherwise keep the process alive until SIGKILL.

stem: An Express 5 route does `res.send(body)`, so Express adds a weak `ETag` automatically. A test first fetches the URL and saves the ETag, then requests it again with that value. With `http.get(url, { headers: { 'If-None-Match': etag } })` the server answers `304`. With `fetch(url, { headers: { 'If-None-Match': etag } })` it answers `200` with the full body. Why?

options.text: Weak ETags (`W/"…"`) never match in conditional requests, and `http.get` returns 304 by mistake
options.why: Express compares weak ETags for `If-None-Match`, and the `http.get` request did get a correct 304.

options.text: `fetch` strips `If-None-Match` from requests because it is a forbidden header name
options.why: `If-None-Match` is not a forbidden header; `fetch` sends it unchanged.

options.text: Setting `If-None-Match` makes `fetch` add `Cache-Control: no-cache`, which Express's freshness check honours
options.why: Per the Fetch spec, a manual conditional header switches the request to no-store mode, and Express then sends the full response.

options.text: Express only sends 304 when the handler calls `res.status(304)` itself
options.why: Express computes freshness in `res.send` and switches to 304 on its own.

explanation: `res.send` adds a weak ETag and checks `req.fresh`, which uses the `fresh` package. A fresh request gets a bodyless 304, so the plain `http.get` behaves as expected. The Fetch standard says that when a request in the default cache mode carries a conditional header such as `If-None-Match`, its cache mode becomes "no-store", and that mode appends `Cache-Control: no-cache`. `fresh` treats a `no-cache` request as one that must get a full response, so Express returns 200 and runs the handler again. Verified with Node 24 and Express 5.2: `http.get` got 304, while `fetch` sent `cache-control: no-cache` and got 200. When you test caching with `fetch`, rely on its HTTP cache, or use `http.request` or undici's `request()` to send raw conditional headers.
reference: Fetch Standard (HTTP-network-or-cache fetch); Express res.send / req.fresh

stem: A worker calls a flaky partner API with `await fetch(url)`. When the partner stops responding, workers hang for minutes and the queue backs up. Which change gives each call a firm 5-second limit?

options.text: Set `server.requestTimeout = 5000` on the worker's HTTP server
options.why: That limits incoming requests to the server, not outgoing fetch calls.

options.text: Pass `signal: AbortSignal.timeout(5000)` to each `fetch` call
options.why: The signal aborts the request after 5 s, and fetch rejects with a `TimeoutError`.

options.text: Wrap the call in `Promise.race` with a 5-second `setTimeout` that resolves
options.why: The race returns early, but the request keeps running and holding a connection.

options.text: Set `http.globalAgent.timeout = 5000`, since fetch uses the global agent
options.why: fetch uses undici's own pool, not `http.globalAgent`.

explanation: fetch has no overall deadline by default; undici only has long header and body timeouts (300 s each). `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` cancels the request and frees the connection, and the rejection's `name` is `'TimeoutError'` (a user abort gives `'AbortError'`). Combine it with your own cancel signal using `AbortSignal.any([...])`. A bare `Promise.race` hides the problem while the request keeps running.

stem: After upgrading from Node 16 to Node 18, a test client that calls `http://localhost:3000` fails with `connect ECONNREFUSED ::1:3000`. The server listens with `server.listen(3000, '127.0.0.1')`. What changed?

options.text: Node 18 started binding servers to IPv6 only, so `127.0.0.1` is ignored
options.why: Listening on 127.0.0.1 still binds IPv4; the change was on the client side.

options.text: Node 17 began returning DNS results in OS order, so `localhost` resolves to `::1` first
options.why: The client tries IPv6 `::1`, where nothing listens; Node 18 doesn't yet fall back to IPv4.

options.text: Node 18 blocks loopback connections unless `--allow-net` is passed
options.why: Node has no such network permission flag for loopback.

options.text: The `localhost` hostname was removed from Node's built-in DNS resolver
options.why: Name resolution still uses the OS resolver; `localhost` resolves fine, just to IPv6 first.

explanation: Before Node 17, `dns.lookup` reordered results to put IPv4 first. Since Node 17 the default `verbatim` order keeps the OS order, which often lists `::1` first. With a server bound only to IPv4, the client's first and only attempt fails. Node 20 enabled `autoSelectFamily` (Happy Eyeballs) by default, which tries both. Other fixes: listen on `::` (dual-stack), connect to `127.0.0.1`, or use `--dns-result-order=ipv4first`.

stem: To defend against Slowloris, a team sets `server.headersTimeout = 2000`. In a test, a client that sends half a request line and then goes silent stays connected for close to 30 seconds before getting `408`. Why?

options.text: `headersTimeout` only counts time after the request line has been completed
options.why: It covers receiving the whole header block, request line included.

options.text: Node enforces the larger of `headersTimeout` and `keepAliveTimeout`
options.why: There is no such rule; the two timeouts are independent.

options.text: Node checks these timeouts on a timer, `connectionsCheckingInterval`, which defaults to 30 s
options.why: Expired connections are only found when the periodic check runs.

options.text: Slow clients are allowed one free retry period before the timeout applies
options.why: There is no grace period; detection depends on the check interval.

explanation: Since Node 18, `headersTimeout` and `requestTimeout` are enforced by a sweep that runs every `connectionsCheckingInterval` milliseconds (30000 by default). A client can therefore last up to the timeout plus one interval. For tight limits, pass a smaller interval when creating the server, for example `http.createServer({ connectionsCheckingInterval: 1000, headersTimeout: 2000 })`. A reverse proxy in front is the more common defence.

stem: Match each protocol with how it carries requests or messages.

options.text: One request at a time per connection, so clients open several connections per host
Many concurrent streams interleaved over a single TCP connection
Streams over QUIC on UDP, so one lost packet doesn't stall the other streams
Full-duplex messages over one connection after an HTTP Upgrade handshake

explanation: HTTP/1.1 keep-alive reuses a connection but can't interleave requests (pipelining is effectively unused). HTTP/2 multiplexes streams over one TCP connection, but a lost TCP packet still stalls all of them (TCP head-of-line blocking). HTTP/3 moves to QUIC, where loss affects only the stream it belongs to. WebSockets upgrade an HTTP/1.1 connection into a long-lived, two-way message channel.
reference: MDN: Evolution of HTTP; RFC 9113; RFC 9114; RFC 6455

stem: A Socket.IO chat app runs on 4 Node instances behind a round-robin load balancer. Many clients fail to connect, and the logs show `400 Bad Request` with `Session ID unknown`. What fixes it?

options.text: Raise each instance's `maxHttpBufferSize` so the handshake fits in one request
options.why: The handshake is small; the problem is which instance receives it.

options.text: Turn on sticky sessions, then add the Redis adapter so instances can broadcast to each other
options.why: Polling requests in one session must reach the same instance; the adapter shares events.

options.text: Switch the load balancer to least-connections so the busiest instance is skipped
options.why: Any non-sticky algorithm still sends a session's requests to different instances.

options.text: Raise the ping timeout so the session survives until the right instance answers
options.why: The session isn't timing out; the instance that gets the request has never seen it.

explanation: Socket.IO starts with HTTP long-polling, which is a series of separate HTTP requests for one session ID. With round-robin balancing those requests land on instances that don't know the session, so they return 400. Use sticky sessions (cookie or IP based), or force `transports: ['websocket']`. Then use an adapter such as `@socket.io/redis-adapter` so a message emitted on one instance reaches sockets connected to the others.

stem: A WebSocket server built on the `ws` library shows thousands of "connected" clients that stopped sending anything hours ago. Most were mobile phones that lost signal. What is the standard fix?

options.text: Set `server.keepAliveTimeout` so idle WebSocket connections are closed
options.why: After the upgrade the socket no longer belongs to the HTTP keep-alive logic.

options.text: Rely on the client's `close` frame, which phones send when they lose signal
options.why: A dropped network sends nothing; that is why the connections are half-open.

options.text: Send pings on an interval and `terminate()` any socket that didn't pong since the last one
options.why: A heartbeat finds dead peers that never sent a close frame or a TCP FIN.

options.text: Lower the OS TCP keepalive interval to one second for all sockets
options.why: OS keepalive can help, but its defaults take hours, and it doesn't check the app is alive.

explanation: When a network path disappears, neither side is told, so the server keeps a half-open connection with its memory and subscriptions. The `ws` docs recommend a heartbeat: mark each socket alive on `pong`, and every N seconds `terminate()` the ones that didn't answer, then `ping()` the rest. Heartbeats also keep NAT and proxy idle timers from silently dropping quiet but healthy connections.
reference: ws docs: How to detect and close broken connections

options.text: The client gets `500`, because `writeHead` overrides the earlier implicit status
options.why: The status line went out with the first `write`, so it can't be overridden.

options.text: The client gets `200`, and the server logs `ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT`
options.why: The first write sent an implicit 200; the later `writeHead` throws.

options.text: The client gets `500`, and nothing is logged, because the call is ignored
options.why: `writeHead` after the headers are sent throws; it isn't silently ignored.

options.text: The connection is reset, because changing the status mid-response is a protocol error
options.why: Node prevents the change by throwing; the response still finishes normally.

explanation: The first `res.write` commits the headers with the default `statusCode` of 200 and `Transfer-Encoding: chunked`. From then on the status can't change. That is why streaming responses can't report a late failure through the status code. They either decide the status before the first byte, or abort the connection with `res.destroy(err)` so the client sees an incomplete response.

stem: An Express app adds `app.use(compression())` globally. Its Server-Sent Events endpoint still returns `200`, but clients now get events in bursts every few seconds instead of immediately. Why?

options.text: Compressed responses must have a `Content-Length`, so Express buffers the whole stream
options.why: Compressed responses are sent chunked; no length is needed.

options.text: The gzip stream buffers output until enough data collects, holding small events back
options.why: Small writes sit in the compressor until a buffer fills, unless you flush after each event.

options.text: `EventSource` can't decompress responses, so it retries until it gets plain text
options.why: Browsers decompress SSE responses transparently.

options.text: The middleware changes `Content-Type` to `application/gzip`, which slows parsing
options.why: Compression adds `Content-Encoding: gzip` and leaves `Content-Type` alone.

explanation: Compressors work on blocks. For a stream of tiny messages, gzip waits for more input, so events are delayed. With the `compression` middleware, call `res.flush()` after each event, or skip compression for `text/event-stream` with its `filter` option. Proxies cause the same symptom; Nginx needs `X-Accel-Buffering: no` or `proxy_buffering off` for SSE.
reference: expressjs/compression docs: res.flush(); MDN: Server-sent events

stem: A Fastify 5 route declares a response schema for `200` with properties `id` and `name`. A developer adds `email` to the object the handler returns, but `email` never appears in responses. Why?

options.text: Fastify only serializes properties that are strings, and `email` is an object
options.why: The property type doesn't matter; whether the schema declares it does.

options.text: Fastify serializes via the response schema, which drops undeclared fields
options.why: fast-json-stringify only writes the properties the schema lists.

options.text: The handler must call `reply.send()` explicitly before properties can be added
options.why: Returning the object from an async handler works the same as `reply.send()`.

options.text: Fastify caches the first response for each route, so later fields are ignored
options.why: Fastify doesn't cache responses; each one is serialized afresh.

explanation: Fastify compiles each response schema into a serializer (fast-json-stringify). It is fast because it knows the shape in advance, and it only outputs declared properties. Fastify presents this as a safety feature against accidentally leaking fields such as `passwordHash`. Add new fields to the schema, or remove the schema if you really want to send arbitrary objects.

stem: An Express 5 app uses the default query parser. A request arrives for `/search?filter[status]=open`. What is `Object.keys(req.query)[0]`? Type the exact key.
explanation: Express 5 changed the default `query parser` setting from `extended` (the `qs` library) to `simple` (Node's `querystring`). Bracket syntax is no longer expanded into nested objects, so the key is the literal string `filter[status]`. Apps that relied on nested queries must set `app.set('query parser', 'extended')`, ideally with input validation, since nested parsing has been a source of prototype-pollution bugs.

stem: An upload endpoint uses `multer({ storage: multer.memoryStorage() })` with no limits. Users upload videos of up to 2 GB, and the pods are being OOM-killed. Which two changes address the cause? (Choose two.)

options.text: Stream the file to object storage or disk instead of holding it in memory
options.why: Memory storage puts the whole file in a Buffer, so each upload needs as much RAM as its size.

options.text: Set `limits: { fileSize }` so oversized uploads are rejected early
options.why: Multer and busboy stop reading and report an error once the limit is crossed.

options.text: Increase `express.json({ limit })` so large uploads are accepted
options.why: Multipart bodies don't go through the JSON parser at all.

options.text: Raise `--max-old-space-size` to 4096 so a 2 GB Buffer fits
options.why: Buffers live outside the V8 heap, and several uploads at once still exhaust RAM.

options.text: Convert each file to base64 first so it uses less memory
options.why: Base64 makes data about 33% larger, not smaller.

explanation: Memory storage is fine for avatars, not for videos. Stream large files straight to their destination with busboy, multer disk storage or a direct-to-S3 stream. Even better for big media, have the client upload to a presigned URL so your servers never handle the bytes. Always set limits on file size, number of files and fields, because a bounded parser is the first defence against memory exhaustion.
reference: multer docs: limits and storage; busboy docs

options.text: Add `keepalive: true` to the fetch options so connections are reused
options.why: In fetch, `keepalive` lets a request outlive the page; it doesn't release bodies.

options.text: Call `res.clone()` before reading `ok`, so the original response is freed
options.why: Cloning tees the body, so there are now two unread copies to hold.

options.text: Consume or cancel each body, for example `await res.body?.cancel()`
options.why: undici only releases a connection once its body is read or cancelled, not by waiting for garbage collection.

options.text: Switch from fetch to `http.get`, which drops unread bodies automatically
options.why: `http.get` behaves the same way: unread responses keep their socket busy.

explanation: An unread response body keeps its connection busy. undici's documentation warns that relying on garbage collection to clean up such bodies leads to excessive connection usage and can stall the pool. If you only need the status, cancel the body (`res.body?.cancel()`), or use a `HEAD` request when the target supports it. Otherwise read it with `res.arrayBuffer()` or `res.text()`.
reference: undici docs: Garbage Collection (consuming response bodies)

stem: Service A calls service B through a keep-alive `http.Agent`. B uses the default 5-second `keepAliveTimeout`. A few `POST /charge` calls per hour fail with `ECONNRESET` as soon as they are sent. Some developers want to retry every failed request automatically. What is the safest approach?

options.text: Set `keepAliveMsecs: 1000` on A's agent so idle sockets close after one second
options.why: `keepAliveMsecs` sets the TCP keepalive probe delay; it doesn't close idle sockets.

options.text: Retry every request that fails with `ECONNRESET`, whatever its method
options.why: A non-idempotent POST may already have run on B before the reset, so it could charge twice.

options.text: Retry only on reused sockets, and make POSTs idempotent with keys
options.why: The race hits reused sockets; idempotency keys make the retry of a POST safe.

options.text: Disable keep-alive on A so each call opens a fresh connection
options.why: That avoids the race, but every call pays a full TCP (and TLS) handshake.

explanation: This is the keep-alive race: B closes an idle socket just as A writes a new request on it. Node's docs suggest checking `request.reusedSocket` and retrying on `ECONNRESET`, since a reset on a reused socket usually means the server never saw the request. That reasoning is only sound for idempotent requests, or POSTs protected by an idempotency key that B checks. Also give A's idle timeout a value shorter than B's `keepAliveTimeout`.

options.text: Call `res.end()` to finish the response cleanly so the client keeps the partial file
options.why: Ending normally makes a truncated CSV look like a complete download.

options.text: If `res.headersSent` is true, call `next(err)` so Express closes the connection
options.why: The default handler destroys the socket, so the client sees a failed download.

options.text: Set `res.statusCode = 500` without sending a body, so the client sees the error
options.why: The status line has already been sent; changing the property has no effect.

options.text: Wrap `res.json` in `try/catch` and ignore the error, since the client has gone
options.why: The client is often still there, waiting on a response that never ends.

explanation: Express's docs say: if you call `next()` with an error after you have started writing the response, the default error handler closes the connection and fails the request. Custom handlers should start with `if (res.headersSent) return next(err);`. For streams, prefer `stream.pipeline(source, transform, res, cb)` so a source error destroys the response instead of leaving it half-written.
reference: Express docs: Error handling (The default error handler)

stem: Which statements about `server.close()` on an HTTP server in Node.js 20 and later are true? (Choose three.)

options.text: It stops the server from accepting new connections
options.why: The listening socket closes at once, so new connection attempts are refused.

options.text: It closes idle keep-alive connections right away
options.why: Since Node 19, `close()` calls `closeIdleConnections()` for you.

options.text: Requests already in progress may finish before the callback fires
options.why: The callback waits until every connection has closed, including active ones.

options.text: It immediately destroys sockets that have a request in progress
options.why: Only `closeAllConnections()` cuts active requests short.

options.text: It answers queued requests with `503 Service Unavailable` automatically
options.why: Node sends no response on your behalf; there is no request queue to answer.

options.text: It waits for clients to close their own idle keep-alive connections first
options.why: That was the behaviour before Node 19, which delayed shutdowns by up to `keepAliveTimeout`.

explanation: Before Node 19, one idle keep-alive connection could keep `server.close()` from finishing until its timeout. Now `close()` drops idle connections at once and lets active requests complete; the callback runs once all connections are gone. `closeAllConnections()` is the hard stop for when your shutdown deadline expires. Remember that active keep-alive clients may still send one more request before their socket closes.

stem: A report endpoint runs a 20-second database query. Users often close the tab early, but the queries still run to completion and overload the database. How can the handler reliably detect that the client went away and cancel the work?

options.text: Listen for `req.on('end')`, which fires when the client disconnects
options.why: `end` fires when the request body has been fully read, which is right away for a GET.

options.text: Check `req.complete` every second and stop when it becomes false
options.why: `req.complete` reports whether the request message arrived in full; it doesn't track the client later.

options.text: Listen for `res.on('close')`; if `res.writableEnded` is false, abort the query
options.why: `close` fires when the connection drops; `writableEnded` tells it apart from a normal finish.

options.text: Wrap the query in `try/catch`; Node throws into the handler when the socket closes
options.why: Node doesn't interrupt running code; nothing is thrown into your handler.

explanation: `res` emits `close` both after a normal response and when the connection is lost; `res.writableEnded` (or `!res.writableFinished`) separates the two cases. Wire it to an `AbortController` and pass the signal to cancellable work, such as a `pg` query cancel or a downstream fetch. In current Node, `req`'s `close` fires as soon as the request body is consumed, so it is a poor disconnect signal for GETs.

stem: Match each TLS-related setting or mechanism with what it does for a Node.js HTTPS client or server.

options.text: Sends the target hostname in the handshake so one IP can serve many certificates
Negotiates the application protocol, such as `h2` or `http/1.1`, during the handshake
Turns off certificate verification, leaving connections open to interception
Adds extra trusted root CAs, such as a corporate CA, on top of the bundled ones

explanation: SNI is why a shared load balancer can present the right certificate for each domain. ALPN is how HTTP/2 is agreed over TLS. Disabling verification is the classic "fix" for self-signed or corporate certificates, and it lets anyone on the path impersonate the server. The right fix is to trust the extra CA with `NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS` (read at process start) or a `ca` option.

stem: A browser client has a 30-second timeout. It calls an ALB with a 60-second idle timeout, which forwards to a Node handler that takes 90 seconds and never checks for disconnects. Node uses default server settings. What does the user see, and what happens on the server?

options.text: The user waits 90 s and gets the result, because each hop resets its timer
options.why: The client gives up at 30 s; nothing extends its own timeout.

options.text: Node's `requestTimeout` kills the handler after 60 s, and the ALB returns 504
options.why: `requestTimeout` only limits receiving the request, and it defaults to 300 s.

options.text: The client gives up at 30 s, and Node keeps working the full 90 s
options.why: Nothing tells the handler; the ALB times out at 60 s, and the result is thrown away.

options.text: The ALB returns 504 to the user at 60 s, and Node stops when the ALB disconnects
options.why: The user left at 30 s, and Node doesn't stop work on its own.

explanation: Each layer has its own timer, and the shortest one decides what the user sees. Nothing propagates cancellation unless you build it, so the server wastes 90 seconds of capacity on an abandoned request. Align the timeouts so that the inner ones are shorter, add a server-side deadline (or a timeout middleware), watch `res.on('close')` to abort early, and turn long work into a 202-accepted job with polling.
reference: AWS docs: ALB idle timeout; Node.js docs: server timeouts

options.text: Decorators are only available inside `onRequest` hooks, not in route handlers
options.why: Decorators are available anywhere in the context they belong to.

options.text: Each `register` creates a context, and the decorator stays inside `dbPlugin`
options.why: Encapsulation keeps it out of sibling contexts; wrap the plugin with `fastify-plugin`.

options.text: `decorate` must be awaited, so the routes are registered before it finishes
options.why: `decorate` is synchronous; the problem is scope, not timing.

options.text: Fastify 5 removed `decorate`; plugins must assign `fastify.db` directly
options.why: `decorate` still exists and is the recommended API.

explanation: Fastify's plugin system is a tree of encapsulated contexts. Decorators, hooks and plugins registered inside one are visible to its children, but not to its parent or siblings. Wrap shared infrastructure (database, auth, config) with `fastify-plugin` (`fp(dbPlugin)`) to skip encapsulation and expose it to the parent. Keep feature plugins encapsulated, so their hooks don't leak into other routes.

stem: You are writing a Server-Sent Events endpoint by hand in Node.js. It runs behind Nginx and an ALB, and some updates arrive minutes apart. Which three things are needed for it to work reliably? (Choose three.)

options.text: Respond with `Content-Type: text/event-stream` and keep the response open
options.why: EventSource requires this type and reads the stream as events arrive.

options.text: End every event with a blank line, as in `data: {...}\n\n`
options.why: The blank line tells EventSource the event is complete; without it nothing is dispatched.

options.text: Send a comment line such as `: ping` every 15 to 30 seconds
options.why: Heartbeats stop proxies and load balancers from closing an idle-looking stream.

options.text: Set `Content-Length` to the total size of the events you expect to send
options.why: A stream has no known length; setting one makes the client stop reading early.

options.text: Upgrade the connection with `Connection: Upgrade` before writing events
options.why: That is the WebSocket handshake; SSE stays an ordinary HTTP response.

options.text: Encode every `data` field as JSON, which the protocol requires
options.why: Data is plain text; JSON is a common convention, not a rule.

explanation: An SSE response is a long-lived `text/event-stream` body made of `field: value` lines, with each event terminated by a blank line. Intermediaries kill connections that look idle (the ALB after 60 s by default), so send comment heartbeats. Also disable proxy buffering (`X-Accel-Buffering: no` for Nginx), avoid compression or flush after each event, and send `id:` fields so reconnecting clients can resume with `Last-Event-ID`.
reference: HTML spec: Server-sent events; MDN: Using server-sent events

stem: A team enables HTTP/2 with `http2.createServer()` (no TLS) behind no proxy. `curl --http2-prior-knowledge` works, but browsers fail to connect at all. What is going on?

options.text: Browsers need `http2.createServer({ allowHTTP1: true })` to enable HTTP/2
options.why: `allowHTTP1` is an option for secure servers, and it adds HTTP/1.1 fallback rather than enabling h2.

options.text: Browsers use HTTP/2 only over TLS; this server speaks cleartext HTTP/2
options.why: Use `createSecureServer` with a certificate; ALPN then negotiates `h2`, or HTTP/1.1 with `allowHTTP1`.

options.text: Node's `node:http2` module is experimental and browsers reject its frames
options.why: `node:http2` has been stable for years and interoperates with browsers.

options.text: HTTP/2 needs UDP, and the firewall blocks UDP traffic from browsers
options.why: HTTP/2 runs over TCP; UDP is used by HTTP/3 (QUIC).

explanation: Every major browser implements HTTP/2 only over TLS, using ALPN to agree on `h2`. A cleartext h2 server (`h2c`) works with tools that assume HTTP/2 from the first byte, but a browser sends HTTP/1.1, which a plain `http2.createServer()` can't understand. Use `http2.createSecureServer({ key, cert, allowHTTP1: true })`. In production, TLS and HTTP/2 often end at the load balancer or CDN, and Node speaks HTTP/1.1 behind it.

stem: A client POSTs a small body to a `node:http` server. The handler reads the body, then calls `res.writeHead(200)` and `res.end('ok')`. Put the events in the order they happen on the server.

options.text: The server's `request` event runs the handler
The request stream emits `end` after the whole body is read
`res.writeHead(200)` queues the status line and headers
The response emits `finish` once all data has been handed to the OS
The response emits `close` when the response is fully done

explanation: The handler starts as soon as the headers are parsed, often before the body has arrived, so body-reading code must wait for `end` (or use `for await`). `finish` means Node has flushed the response to the operating system, not that the client received it. `close` follows, and it is also the event you get when a connection drops early, which is why you check `writableEnded` in a `close` listener.
reference: Node.js docs: http.IncomingMessage and http.ServerResponse events

stem: Setting `server.timeout = 0` on a Node.js HTTP server also disables `server.requestTimeout`, so slow clients can take as long as they like to send a request.

options.text: True
options.why: `server.timeout` is the socket inactivity timeout; `requestTimeout` is enforced separately.

options.text: False
options.why: `server.timeout` already defaults to 0, while `requestTimeout` stays at 300 s until you change it.

explanation: `server.timeout` (default 0) is a socket inactivity timeout. `requestTimeout` (default 300000 ms) and `headersTimeout` (default 60000 ms) are independent limits on receiving the request, added to protect against slow-client attacks. To allow very long uploads you must raise `requestTimeout` itself, and setting it to 0 removes that protection, so do it only behind a proxy that enforces its own limits.
